structure.title: An inquiry among friends
structure.text: Utterson follows troubling connections through conversations, documents, and encounters that supply incomplete evidence.

structure.title: Accounts withheld
structure.text: Later testimony changes how earlier events can be understood. The order in which explanations arrive is central to the story.

people.name: Mr Hyde
people.text: A disturbing figure connected to Jekyll's affairs.

context.title: Protecting reputation
context.text: Discretion is a social virtue among Utterson's friends. It can preserve trust while making direct questions difficult.
context.takeaway: Silence can protect more than one thing.

context.title: Documents as evidence
context.text: Wills, letters, and statements organise the investigation. Their authority depends partly on who can read them and when.

notice.why: The architecture separates respectable appearance from private activity.
Strong reactions can exceed the witnesses' ability to explain them.

opening: A respectable doctor changes his will to leave everything to a man his friends find repulsive. Nobody can explain the connection, and the doctor refuses to discuss it. His lawyer suspects blackmail and begins asking questions, hoping to rescue a friend’s reputation before something worse happens. Stevenson follows that investigation through locked doors, evasive answers, and a London where respectability offers very little assurance about what a person might be capable of when nobody is watching.
